formNote: Mojidata IDS: ⿰彳𢛳. The Shuowen: 德，升也, “to rise”; it also lists 惪, 外得於人，內得於己也, “gained from others outwardly, gained in oneself inwardly”, a gloss by sound with 得, “to get”.
summary: Virtue in the old sense of power: the efficacy a thing or person has by being what it is. The Daodejing is the classic of the Way (道) and its power (德); Confucians made it moral character.
placement: At the summit of the Rössler fold, the one place where the flow rises: the Shuowen glosses 德 as 升, “to rise”. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: To Rise; to Get
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen glosses 德 as 升, “to rise”, and glosses its variant 惪 as what is gained outwardly from others and inwardly in oneself (外得於人，內得於己). Virtue as what one has come to possess.
satellites.caveat: Glosses by sound (德 / 得); they record Han understanding, not origin.

satellites.title: The Highest Virtue Is Not Virtuous
satellites.evidence: Daodejing ch. 38: 上德不德，是以有德；下德不失德，是以無德 — “the highest virtue does not cling to virtue, and so has it; the lowest never lets go of virtue, and so lacks it.” Power that is held on to is lost.

satellites.title: Excellence, Elsewhere
satellites.evidence: Greek ἀρετή is the excellence of a thing at being what it is: a knife’s sharpness, a horse’s speed, a person’s virtue. Like 德, it names a power before it names a morality.
satellites.caveat: An analogy, not a translation. The two systems differ greatly, and no early text renders one by the other.
